hints: Look at the left diagram of the picornavirus in Fig. 1.1 - what are the two layers you can see, an outer ring of circles and a coiled structure inside?
Think about what makes a virus different from a cell - does it have cytoplasm, organelles and a cell surface membrane, or is it much simpler and unable to carry out metabolism on its own?
walkthrough:
What You Actually See In The Diagram**
Think of a virus as a parcel, not a cell. The outer ring of small circles in Fig. 1.1 is a protein coat called the capsid. Inside is the coiled-up genetic material, which is a core of nucleic acid, either DNA or RNA.

Why A Virus Is Not A Cell**
A virus has no cytoplasm, no organelles and no metabolic machinery, so it is described as acellular. That is why it cannot replicate on its own and must enter a host cell like the mammal or bird cell here.
Final answer: Protein coat / capsid surrounding a core of nucleic acid (DNA or RNA); acellular.

hints: Start by comparing the two numbers given - the virus is $30\text{nm}$ in diameter, but what is the smallest separation a light microscope can resolve?
Recall why that limit exists - what property of visible light sets the resolution limit at about $200\text{nm}$?
Put the comparison together to make a clear yes or no decision - is $30\text{nm}$ large enough to disturb light waves and be resolved?
walkthrough:
Resolution Is The Key Idea**
Resolution means the ability to see two close points as separate. A light microscope can only separate points that are about $200\text{nm}$ or more apart.

Compare Virus Size To That Limit**
The picornavirus is only $30\text{nm}$ in diameter, which is much smaller than $200\text{nm}$. Visible light has a relatively long wavelength, so such a tiny particle cannot interfere with light waves enough to form an image.

Make The Decision**
Because the virus is well below the resolution limit, the answer is no, it cannot be seen with the light microscope. You would need an electron microscope with its much shorter wavelength and higher resolution.

Final answer: No; resolution of light microscope is too low / not high enough as it can only distinguish objects $200\text{nm}$ or more apart; $30\text{nm}$ virus is too small / wavelength of light too long to be resolved.

hints: Follow the first arrow in Fig. 1.1 - what is the virus touching on the host cell surface membrane before the membrane starts to curve?
Think about why only certain viruses enter certain cells - what must match between the virus capsid proteins and the host membrane proteins?
Look at the middle and right diagrams - how does the membrane move around the virus and what structure pinches off inside the cell?
walkthrough:
Attachment By Specific Binding**
The virus first attaches to receptor proteins in the host cell surface membrane. This is specific because the capsid proteins and the receptors have complementary shapes, so only the correct host cell will be recognised.

Engulfing By The Membrane**
Once bound, the host membrane infolds and curves around the virus. This uptake of a solid particle by infolding of membrane is endocytosis.

Pinching Off Inside**
In the right-hand diagram the membrane has completely surrounded the virus and pinched in to form a vesicle (a membrane-bound sac) inside the cytoplasm, with the virus still attached to receptors in the vesicle membrane.
Final answer: Virus binds to specific / complementary receptors on host cell surface membrane; membrane infolds by endocytosis and pinches off to form a vesicle containing the virus inside the cell.
